newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Congress on collision course over IRS.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Congress on collision course over IRS.

text.p: The Clinton administration and Congress appear to be on a collision course over how best to reform the widely reviled Internal Revenue Service.
A congressionally appointed commission will recommend this month the establishment of an independent board to oversee the tax collection agency, the panel's top official said Tuesday.
But Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers, the administration's point man on IRS reform, attacked the idea, calling it "dangerously flawed."
Jeffrey Trinca, chief of staff for the National Commission on Restructuring the Internal Revenue Sevice, said the board was needed to improve the expertise of the IRS and make it more accountable.

Under the commission's plan, which is expected to be formally unveiled June 25, the seven-person board would be comprised of five private citizens appointed by the president and approved by the Senate, and two govermnment officials.
"The role of the board of directors would be to guide the direction of the IRS," Trinca told the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants.
"It will not be involved in the particulars of tax cases," he told reporters later.
Right now, Trinca argued, it is not clear who exactly is in charge of the IRS -- the Treasury Secretary, the agency's commissioner or someone else.

Under the panel's proposal, the independent board would be the one responsible and would appoint the IRS commissioner, not the administration. Trinca added that he expects Congress to move ahead quickly on translating the programme into law.
But Summers told the accountants the panel proposal risked undermining the ability of the IRS to collect taxes just as the agency is showing signs of improvement.

"Giving unelected citizens who may earn private salaries utimate power over ... administration of tax policy would move the IRS further away from the control of the American people," Summers said. "These proposals pose an unacceptable risk to our nation's revenue stream," he added.

The administration has put forward its own plan for improving the workings of the IRS. Under that proposal, the president would name a board of government officials to oversee the tax collection agency. A separate board of private-sector experts would also be established to provide advice.
